title: Effects of Caffeine Mouth Rinse on Cognitive Performance and Psychological Responses in Trained Individuals: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background: Caffeine mouth rinse (Caf-MR) has been investigated as a non-ingestive strategy that may influence cognitive performance and psychological responses. However, evidence in trained individuals remains limited, and psychological responses have not been comprehensively synthesized. This systematic review evaluated the effects of Caf-MR on cognitive performance and psychological responses in trained individuals. Methods: Six electronic databases were searched through 24 September 2026 for randomized controlled studies comparing Caf-MR with a non-caffeinated placebo or control. Reference lists of relevant reviews and eligible studies were also screened. Owing to heterogeneity in protocols and outcomes, findings were synthesized qualitatively. Results: Ten studies were included; five assessed cognitive outcomes and six psychological responses, with one study contributing to both domains. Cognitive findings were heterogeneous, with improvements observed in selected reaction-time measures and Stroop interference time, as well as fewer errors during a sport-specific cognitive-motor task, while other reaction-time and accuracy outcomes showed no clear benefit. Among psychological studies, only one reported a Caf-MR-specific increase in felt arousal, with no consistent effects on mood, motivation, mental effort, mental fatigue, or enjoyment. Methodological quality ranged from fair to good, and all studies had some concerns regarding overall risk of bias. Conclusions: Overall, despite improvements in selected cognitive outcomes, current evidence remains insufficient to establish consistent cognitive or psychological benefits of Caf-MR in trained individuals. Future research should prioritize assessing blinding effectiveness, comparing Caf-MR protocols under standardized experimental conditions, and using comparable outcome measures to clarify potential differences across tasks and contexts.

title: Long-Term Add-On Use of a Fixed Multicomponent Formulation Containing Palmitoylethanolamide and Acetyl-L-Carnitine in Fibromyalgia Syndrome: A 15-Month Retrospective Single-Cohort Study of 150 Patients.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Long-term treatment options for fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) remain limited and there is a lack of real-world data on the extended use of nutraceutical formulations containing palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) and acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC). This study describes a cohort treated for 12 months with a fixed multicomponent formulation containing PEA and ALC, followed by an additional visit three months post-treatment. Methods: This retrospective, uncontrolled single-cohort study involved 150 consecutive adults diagnosed with fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS). Participants received a fixed oral formulation comprising palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) 600 mg, acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC) 500 mg, Boswellia serrata 100 mg, vitamin B6 and vitamin E, administered twice daily as an adjunct to stable background therapy. Pain levels were assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), and the impact of the disease was evaluated with the revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQR) over a period of up to 15 months. Sleep quality was measured using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) for up to 6 months. Missing data were addressed through various methods, including a mixed model, last observation carried forward, delta-adjusted and baseline-carried-forward scenarios, as well as non-responder imputation. Results: Sixty-four patients completed the 12-month course, 45 discontinued (36 for perceived lack of efficacy) and 41 were lost to follow-up. Estimated mean VAS fell from 76.3 to 52.3 at 12 months and FIQR from 73.6 to 56.1; under the worst-case assumption that every non-completer returned to baseline, the mean 12-month change in VAS was -13.0 points (95% CI -15.9 to -10.2). At 6 months, 78.1% of completers reached the FIQR minimal clinically important difference and 59.4% the IMMPACT 30% pain threshold, corresponding to 37.3% and 28.7% of all 150 patients with non-responder imputation; only 20.3% of completers (10.0% of all patients) improved by ≥3 PSQI points. Recorded adverse events occurred in 10.0% of patients. Retention at 12 months was 60.6% (42.7% if patients lost to follow-up were counted as discontinuations). In completers, pain and FIQR three months after the end of treatment were within one point of the 12-month values. Conclusions: In this uncontrolled cohort, 12 months of add-on treatment with a multicomponent formulation containing PEA and ALC was associated with reductions in pain and disease impact, whereas sleep outcomes changed minimally. However, attrition was substantial and partially response-dependent; therefore, the observed changes cannot be attributed to the formulation or its individual components. These descriptive findings support the need for a controlled trial with a duration of at least 12 months.

title: Diet and the Food Allergy Exposome Across the Lifespan: Nutritional Transitions, Microbiome-Immune Pathways, and Emerging Clinical Phenotypes.
abstract: Food allergy is increasingly recognized across geographic regions and age groups, although temporal trends are difficult to separate from differences in diagnostic criteria and surveillance. This narrative review examines how diet and nutrition interact with the wider exposome to influence food allergy risk, oral tolerance, and clinical phenotypes across the lifespan. We critically synthesize evidence on early-life allergen introduction, dietary diversity, fiber and microbial metabolites, Westernized and ultra-processed dietary patterns, epithelial barrier dysfunction, medication exposures, pollution, and changing food systems. Randomized trials support early peanut introduction and, with greater heterogeneity, early egg introduction as preventive approaches; by contrast, causal evidence linking most other nutritional and environmental exposures to clinically confirmed food allergy remains limited. The diet-microbiome-immune axis offers plausible pathways connecting dietary substrates and microbial metabolites to epithelial integrity and immune regulation, but human mechanistic and longitudinal evidence remains incomplete. Globalization, migration, alternative protein sources, and climate-related exposures may reshape allergen encounters. Adult-onset food allergy, pollen-food allergy syndrome, alpha-gal syndrome, and cofactor-dependent reactions further illustrate how environmental influences may alter clinical expression beyond infancy. We propose an integrated life-course framework linking nutritional and non-nutritional exposures, underlying biological pathways, and emerging allergic phenotypes, while explicitly distinguishing intervention-supported findings from observational associations and mechanistic hypotheses. Future studies should combine standardized clinical outcomes with dietary assessment, environmental exposure measurements, functional microbiome profiling, metabolomics, and immune phenotyping to identify modifiable pathways relevant to food allergy prevention.

title: The Circadian Diet in Age-Related Neurodegeneration: Nutrient Timing, Sleep, and Mitochondrial Mechanisms.
abstract: Circadian rhythms coordinate sleep-wake regulation, endocrine secretion, nutrient handling and cellular energy metabolism. Circadian and sleep disturbances are associated with metabolic and cardiovascular morbidity and with neurodegenerative disorders, particularly Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), although whether restoring circadian alignment modifies neurodegeneration remains uncertain. This narrative review examines chrononutrition within the broader context of sleep regulation, physical activity and circadian care, distinguishing evidence from cellular and animal models, observational studies and clinical trials. Meal timing and dietary composition act as signals to peripheral clocks, while NAD+, sirtuins and AMP-activated protein kinase link nutrient availability with clock regulation and mitochondrial metabolism. We appraise time-restricted eating, protein distribution, NAD+ precursors, tryptophan- and melatonin-containing foods, magnesium, omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols and fermentable fiber. Experimental findings provide mechanistic plausibility, but metabolic improvements and target engagement have not translated into demonstrated neuroprotection. Clinical application must account for levodopa-protein interactions, undernutrition, frailty and sarcopenia. Adequately powered trials with circadian-phase assessment, controlled energy intake and clinically meaningful neurological outcomes are required before a "circadian diet" can be established as a disease-modifying intervention.

title: Retinoic Acid Alleviates Accelerated Atherosclerosis in Diesel Exhaust-Derived PM2.5-Exposed ApoE-/- Mice by Enhancing eNOS-NO Coupling.
abstract: Respiratory exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), including diesel exhaust particles (DEPs), is a major air pollutant associated with pulmonary inflammation and cardiovascular diseases. This study investigated the protective effects and underlying mechanisms of retinoic acid (RA) against PM2.5-induced lung injury and accelerated atherosclerosis. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified from lung tissues of five non-smokers and six patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database and analyzed using the L1000CDS2, which identified RA as a candidate therapeutic compound. The Comparative Toxicogenomics Database was subsequently used to investigate curated associations between lung and cardiovascular disorders, suggesting the endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS)/nitric oxide (NO) signaling pathway as a candidate mechanism for experimental validation. ApoE-/- mice were exposed to DEP via a nebulization chamber and treated orally with all-trans retinoic acid (1 or 5 mg/kg/day) for 8 weeks. RA significantly reduced C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 1/2 (CXCL1/2) levels in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and decreased pulmonary expression of Muc5ac, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. RA also lowered blood pressure, improved serum lipid profiles, and attenuated inflammatory cell infiltration and arterial wall thickening in the thoracic aorta. In HUVECs, RA significantly increased guanosine triphosphate (GTP) cyclohydrolase-1 (GTPCH-1) expression, eNOS phosphorylation, tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) levels, and the BH4/BH2 ratio. These findings suggest that the activation of the GTPCH-1/BH4/eNOS coupling pathway contributes to the protective effects of RA against DEP-induced cardiovascular injury.

title: Effects of a Targeted Nutritional Intervention on Auditory-Visual Event-Related Potentials in South-Indian Infants: An Exploratory Analysis of a Cluster Randomized Trial.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Inadequate macronutrient intake may affect neurodevelopment in early infancy. In India, government-supplied take-home rations (THRs) attempt to meet this gap but lack adequate fat and protein. This study evaluated the impact of a 3-month macronutrient modified-THR intervention on infant neurodevelopment using event-related potentials (ERPs). Methods: A two-group cluster randomized controlled trial (village clusters = 12/group; N = 67/group) enrolled healthy breastfed infants (6-9 months) in Karnataka, India. The intervention group received a milk-legume-based THR providing ~200 kcal/day (ML-THR, estimated protein:energy (PE) and fat:energy (FE) ratios: 12% and 45%) with the standard government THR (SG-THR, estimated PE and FE ratios: 7% and 4%), while controls received SG-THRs only. All mothers received education on infant and young child feeding practices, water sanitation and hygiene. Auditory, visual and attention processing ERPs were measured using a short, culturally adapted, infant-friendly paradigm. Linear mixed models evaluated intervention effects over time. Results: The intervention was associated with region-specific visual ERP changes: increased fractional latencies in anterior regions for face, nonface (500-750 ms); decreased fractional latencies in the central region for frequent (10-250 ms) and face (500-750 ms) and in the posterior region for frequent-rare difference (250-500 ms). The intervention group also demonstrated a reduced area under the curve for nonface stimuli (250-500 ms). No significant auditory or visual hemifield effects were observed. None of the observed effects remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Conclusions: The findings are exploratory and suggest the need to examine the effects of improved protein quality and fat content in THRs on visual-cortical processing in larger samples.

title: Cistanche deserticola: A Homology-of-Medicine-and-Food Herb with Intestinal-Moistening and Laxative Effects.
abstract: Cistanche deserticola is a perennial parasitic herb of the Orobanchaceae family and a traditional Chinese medicinal material included in the homology-of-medicine-and-food category. It has traditionally been used to nourish the kidney and essence and to relieve constipation. Recent studies have investigated its potential effects on intestinal motility, gut microbiota, and fecal water regulation. This review summarizes the reported chemical constituents of C. deserticola, including phenylethanoid glycosides, polysaccharides, flavonoids, and sugar alcohols, and examines the available evidence regarding their potential contributions to laxative effects. Possible mechanisms involving intestinal motility, neurotransmitter-related signaling, gut microbiota and microbial metabolites, and aquaporin expression are discussed. Evidence is considered hierarchically: findings from identified C. deserticola preparations are distinguished from indirect findings involving other Cistanche species, isolated compounds, or multi-component herbal formulations, while proposed causal pathways are treated as hypotheses unless directly tested. The evidence base is predominantly preclinical, and human studies are limited; the specific contributions of individual constituents, the causal relationships underlying the proposed mechanisms, and the long-term safety of different preparations remain insufficiently established. This review also discusses challenges in raw-material standardization, evidence-based quality control, and functional food development, highlighting the need for further mechanistic, toxicological, and clinical studies to support the rational development of C. deserticola-based products.

title: Caffeinated Gum Enhances External Work During Perceptually Regulated Cycling in Well-Trained Male Athletes.
abstract: While caffeine may lower ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) or increase power output at a given RPE, whether caffeinated gum produces these effects during perceptually regulated exercise remains unclear. This study examined whether caffeinated gum increases self-selected cycling output at regulated-RPE in well-trained male athletes. Twelve well-trained male athletes (age: 21 ± 2 years; body mass: 77.3 ± 6.0 kg; VO2peak: 47 ± 4 mL/kg/min) completed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trials separated by 7 days. Athletes chewed caffeinated gum (6 mg/kg) or placebo for 15 min before two 10 min cycling stages at RPE 4 and 7 (0-10 OMNI Scale). Cadence, power output, oxygen uptake, heart rate, and blood lactate concentration were measured. Caffeinated gum significantly increased cadence (RPE 4: 72 ± 7 vs. 66 ± 10 rpm, p = 0.02; RPE 7: 77 ± 9 vs. 71 ± 11 rpm, p = 0.04), total work (53 ± 10 vs. 48 ± 10 kJ, p 0.05). Caffeinated gum (6 mg/kg) enhances self-selected cycling work at prescribed RPEs, indicating that it alters perceptually regulated exercise intensity in well-trained males.

title: Trajectory of Psychological Adaptation During an 8-Day Fast: Changes in Subjective Well-Being, Mood, and Neuroendocrine Responses.
abstract: Prolonged fasting induces substantial metabolic and neuroendocrine adaptations; however, less is known about the accompanying psychological changes. This study evaluated changes in subjective well-being and mood during an 8-day fast in relation to serum concentrations of α -endorphin, serotonin, oxytocin, and cortisol. Fifteen male subjects in good health completed an 8-day fast. Subjective well-being was assessed each day using a comparative self-rating scale, and mood was evaluated using the Polish version of the UWIST Mood Adjective Checklist (UMACL). Serum concentrations of α-endorphin, serotonin, oxytocin, and cortisol were measured before and after the fast, both at rest and following a maximal exercise test on an ergometer. Subjective well-being gradually improved during the fasting period, and tense arousal, a dimension of mood, decreased. No significant changes were observed in energetic arousal or hedonic tone. The combination of fasting and exercise was associated with significant increases in α-endorphin, serotonin, and cortisol concentrations. Fasting was associated with a significant increase in post-exercise cortisol concentrations, whereas exercise after fasting was associated with a significant increase in serotonin concentrations. Despite concurrent psychological and hormonal adaptations, no consistent relationships were found between changes in hormone concentrations and psychological variables. Prolonged fasting was accompanied by gradual psychological adaptation, reflected in improved subjective well-being and reduced tension, whereas exercise under these conditions was associated with neurohormonal changes. These changes were associated with the coordinated activation of multiple neuroendocrine systems, suggesting that psychological and neuroendocrine adaptations represent complementary responses to prolonged metabolic stress rather than being opposing processes.

title: Anti-Inflammatory Dietary Supplements in Pregnancy: A Scoping Review.
abstract: This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on the safety and efficacy of anti-inflammatory dietary supplements used during pregnancy, assessing maternal and fetal outcomes. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2016-June 2026), following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (10.17605/osf.io/4kmv9). Eligible studies included human clinical trials and observational studies evaluating anti-inflammatory dietary supplements in pregnant women. Eighty unique studies (96 publications) from 28 countries were included, of which 63 (78.8%) were randomized clinical trials. Thirteen supplement categories were identified. Vitamin D (n = 23) and omega-3 fatty acids (n = 17) accounted for nearly half of all studies; probiotics (n = 11) formed the third-largest category. For these three supplements, most studies reported changes in inflammatory and glycemic markers, primarily in gestational diabetes mellitus and high-risk populations, but adverse events were collected in a minority of studies, so tolerability is documented rather than established. Evidence for zinc, magnesium, and alpha-lipoic acid was limited. Curcumin, chlorella, vitamin E, epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), resveratrol, and ginger were each supported by only one or two studies. Supplementation was initiated in the first trimester in 19 studies (23.8%), and neonatal safety outcomes were reported infrequently. Evidence on anti-inflammatory dietary supplements in pregnancy is concentrated in a few compounds, in a small number of countries, and in biochemical outcomes measured in selected populations. Tolerability was evaluated in only a small number of studies, which limits its use as an indicator of safety. The map highlights the scarcity of controlled studies with prespecified harm outcomes, of first-trimester initiation, and of infant follow-up beyond the first months of life.

title: Maternal HFD and CDAHFD Exposure from Pregnancy to Lactation Differentially Affect Lipid Profiles and Behavior in Offspring Mice.
abstract: Maternal nutritional status during pregnancy and lactation can influence metabolic and neurobehavioral development in offspring. However, the contribution of specific lipid alterations to these effects remains unclear. This study investigated whether maternal exposure to different high-fat diets produces distinct metabolic and neurobehavioral outcomes in offspring. Pregnant ICR mice were fed a control diet, a conventional high-fat diet (HFD), or a 50% choline-deficient, amino acid-defined high-fat diet (50% CDAHFD) from embryonic day 12 until weaning. Male offspring were assessed at 4-6 weeks of age for body weight, plasma lipid levels, behavioral phenotypes, prefrontal neurotransmitter release, and expression of genes related to serotonergic and dopaminergic signaling. A total of 31 dams and 196 offspring were used in the experiments and allocated to each experimental group. Offspring in both HFD and 50% CDAHFD groups exhibited increased body weight and total cholesterol levels compared to controls, whereas plasma triglycerides were elevated a tendency in the 50% CDAHFD group. HFD offspring showed reduced spontaneous locomotor activity, and increased prefrontal serotonin release with altered serotonergic gene expression. Conversely, 50% CDAHFD offspring displayed increased exploratory behavior in the open field test alongside altered dopamine neuron-related genes, without locomotor or social deficits. Exposure of mothers to different high-fat diets has been suggested to cause specific changes in their offspring's lipid profiles, which in turn modulate the serotonin and dopamine systems differently, leading to specific behavioral changes.

title: Time-Restricted Eating as a Dietary Intervention for Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Time-restricted eating (TRE) appears to be a promising dietary strategy for women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), with potential benefits for insulin resistance and metabolic health. Emerging evidence also suggests that TRE may be associated with changes in gut microbiota composition and microbial metabolites, as well as circulating biomarkers involved in metabolic regulation. However, the relationships among these factors remain poorly understood. The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that adding TRE to Healthy Eating Plate recommendations is more effective in improving insulin resistance, assessed using HOMA-IR, than Healthy Eating Plate recommendations alone in women with PMOS. Exploratory analyses will investigate changes in gut microbiota composition, microbial metabolites, and circulating concentrations of neuroactive compounds. This two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial will compare 8-h TRE with unrestricted meal timing in women aged 18 to 40 years with PMOS and a BMI of 25-40 kg/m2 with a 1:1 allocation ratio. Both groups will receive Healthy Eating Plate-based dietary advice and attend four visits; the TRE protocol will be followed for 8 weeks. The primary outcome will be a change in HOMA-IR from baseline to week 8. We will also assess changes in glucose and lipid metabolism, circulating neuroactive compounds, including GABA and kisspeptin, anthropometric parameters, hormonal profile, composition and diversity of the microbiota and its metabolites. We anticipate that this study will expand the limited evidence regarding TRE in women with PMOS and provide exploratory insights into the relationships among gut microbiota composition, microbial metabolites, circulating GABA and kisspeptin, and insulin resistance. The findings may help identify potential mechanisms underlying the metabolic effects of TRE in this population. 1.1, August 2026. NCT06204965. Participant recruitment has not yet commenced.

title: Nutraceutical, Nutritional and Phytotherapeutic Interventions for Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Intellectual Disability: Mechanisms and Clinical Evidence.
abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is frequently accompanied by a range of neuropsychiatric and neurological comorbidities, including anxiety, depression, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), sleep disturbances, and epilepsy. Conventional pharmacological treatments often provide partial relief and may be associated with adverse effects, prompting interest in adjunctive strategies such as phytotherapy. This review examines the current evidence on selected plant-derived compounds-particularly Crocus sativus (saffron), Bacopa monnieri, Curcuma longa (curcumin), and other botanicals-in the management of disorders associated with ID. Mechanistic pathways, clinical evidence, and safety considerations are critically discussed. Although some phytotherapeutic interventions have shown preliminary evidence of potential benefit and may modulate pathways involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and neurotransmitter function, direct clinical evidence in individuals with ID remains limited. Further well-designed randomized controlled trials, particularly in ID-specific populations, are needed to establish efficacy, safety, optimal dosing, and clinical applicability.

title: Disentangling Fat and Sugar in the Western Diet: Parental Consumption of a High-Fat Diet Alters Offspring Brain Development.
abstract: Maternal consumption of the Western diet is a precursor for metabolic conditions such as obesity and is associated with increased offspring risk for neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). It is not clear which component (i.e., high-fat or high-sugar) of the Western diet contributes to changes in offspring neurodevelopment. We used a mouse model of parental consumption of five different diets containing varying levels of fat and sugar to examine and compare their effects on offspring brain structure. Male and female offspring (avg n = 15/sex/diet) were assessed for differences in body weight and developmental milestone achievement, and their brains were imaged at postnatal day (P) 65 using magnetic resonance imaging to compare brain structure. Offspring of the high-fat-only and combined high-fat/high-sugar diet groups showed delayed righting reflex success and heavier weight at weaning. Brain structure differences were also observed in early adulthood (P65), with the pattern of change induced by high-fat/high-sugar diets similar to that observed in some autism mouse models. Parental high-fat-only and combined high-fat/high-sugar diets altered offspring brain structure, but the high-sugar-only diet did not. High fat consumption is likely a key driver of the observed offspring brain changes and is a modifiable risk factor for NDDs.
keywords: Developmental Origins of Health and Disease

title: Nutritional Care of the Frail Patient with Heart Failure: Evidence, Uncertainties and Research Priorities.
abstract: Frailty is highly prevalent in patients with heart failure (HF) and frequently coexists with malnutrition, sarcopenia, cachexia, and obesity, creating substantial challenges for nutritional assessment and management. These conditions overlap clinically but represent distinct biological phenotypes and should not be treated as interchangeable constructs. This narrative review critically synthesizes current evidence on nutritional care in patients with HF and frailty, focusing on nutritional assessment, energy and protein requirements, areas of alignment and conflict between HF- and frailty-oriented recommendations, and the effects of nutritional interventions on frailty-related outcomes. Nutritional assessment should be multidimensional, as congestion, inflammation, altered body composition, and renal dysfunction may limit the interpretability of body weight, BMI, biochemical indices, and screening tools. Current recommendations for energy and protein intake remain largely extrapolated from geriatric, multimorbidity, renal, or general HF populations, and no universally validated targets exist for frail patients with HF. Dietary management therefore requires balancing potentially competing priorities, including congestion control, preservation of muscle mass and function, adequate nutrient intake, renal limitations, and, in obesity-related HF, intentional fat loss without excessive loss of lean tissue. Available interventional evidence suggests that individualized nutritional support may improve nutritional status and selected functional outcomes, but effects on frailty as an integrated syndrome remain uncertain. Overall, nutritional care in HF with frailty should move towards phenotype-directed, multidisciplinary strategies integrating nutrition, physical activity, rehabilitation, and longitudinal assessment. Future trials should standardize frailty definitions, clinically relevant outcomes, and nutrition-related targets.

title: Ishige foliacea Water Extract (KDC22-01) Attenuates Tau Hyperphosphorylation and Ameliorates Scopolamine-Induced Memory Impairment in Mice.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Ishige foliacea is an edible brown alga containing bioactive polyphenols with reported neuroprotective properties. Although extracts of I. foliacea have previously been shown to ameliorate cognitive impairment, their effects on pathological tau phosphorylation remain poorly characterized. This study investigated the neuroprotective and cognition-modulating effects of KDC22-01, an aqueous extract of I. foliacea. Methods: KDC22-01 was chemically characterized by total polyphenol and flavonoid-equivalent contents and HPLC fingerprinting. Its effects on pre-aggregated Aβ25-35-induced cytotoxicity and okadaic acid (OA)-induced tau phosphorylation were evaluated in SH-SY5Y cells. Cognitive performance and hippocampal tau phosphorylation were further assessed in male C57BL/6 mice with scopolamine (SCO)-induced cognitive impairment following oral KDC22-01 administration (100 or 300 mg/kg). Results: KDC22-01 protected SH-SY5Y cells against Aβ25-35-induced cytotoxicity, restoring cell viability from approximately 59% to 87% of control levels at 50 μg/mL. KDC22-01 also reduced the OA-induced p-tau (Ser199)/total tau ratio at 25 and 50 μg/mL. In SCO-treated mice, 100 mg/kg KDC22-01 significantly improved performance in the Morris water maze and passive avoidance test, whereas improvements in Y-maze spontaneous alternation did not reach statistical significance. Both KDC22-01 doses reduced hippocampal p-tau (Ser396), while changes in hippocampal Aβ levels were not statistically significant. Conclusions: These findings suggest that attenuation of tau hyperphosphorylation may contribute to the cognitive effects of KDC22-01 and support further investigation of this aqueous I. foliacea extract as a candidate functional-food ingredient for cognitive health.

title: Boosting Post-Stroke Recovery: The Role of Nutritional Supplementation in Reducing Fatigue-A Single-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Post-stroke fatigue (PSF) remains a debilitating barrier to recovery. Chronic inflammation and oxidative stress often create physiological plateaus that standard rehabilitation alone cannot resolve. This single-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluated the efficacy of Food for Special Medical Purposes formulated with iron and other vitamins and minerals in Sucrosomial® form, allowing improved absorption, bioavailability, and tolerability, as an adjunct to neurorehabilitation. One hundred and twenty stroke patients were randomized into an experimental group (Sid-G) receiving the specific nutraceutical compound or a control group (CG) receiving standard care. Longitudinal assessments from baseline (T0) through 16 weeks (T3) measured clinical outcomes (including fatigue, motor/cognitive function) and physiological markers, specifically phase angle (PhA) derived from Bioimpedance Analysis, and key inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers (IL-6 and MPO). The Sid-G cohort demonstrated superior, sustained improvements in fatigue, motor, and cognitive function (p < 0.05). These clinical gains were reflected in the following physiological observations: the time × group interaction for cellular integrity (SPhA) was not significant, though within-group improvements were observed in Sid-G (p = 0.009); at the group level, significant time × group interactions were detected for key inflammatory and oxidative stress markers (IL-6, p = 0.001; MPO, p = 0.026). Correlational analysis revealed a significant association between changes in inflammatory markers and clinical recovery outcomes in Sid-G, a pattern absent in the CG. Adjunctive supplementation may support recovery by helping patients to overcome physiological plateaus. These findings support further evaluation of an integrated, metabolically focused approach to neurorehabilitation.

title: Targeting Key Mechanisms of Nutraceuticals in Chronic Pain: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Chronic pain (CP) is a major cause of disability worldwide and reflects interactions among multiple pathophysiological mechanisms. Despite the availability of pharmacological therapies, many patients continue to experience inadequate pain control, supporting interest in complementary approaches. Nutraceuticals have been investigated as potential adjuncts because several compounds modulate biological pathways implicated in pain persistence. This narrative review provides a mechanism-based overview of nutraceuticals in CP across five interconnected domains: neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, central sensitization, peripheral sensitization, and descending inhibitory modulation. Literature was identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library, with the final update completed on 8 October 2026; preclinical mechanisms and clinical efficacy were evaluated separately. Earlier short-term trials of alpha-lipoic acid suggested symptomatic improvement in diabetic peripheral neuropathy, whereas a 2024 Cochrane review found little or no benefit after six months. Evidence syntheses suggest possible analgesic effects of palmitoylethanolamide in mixed chronic pain populations and of curcuminoids in knee osteoarthritis. Clinical studies of omega-3 fatty acids also suggest a possible reduction in pain intensity, although substantial heterogeneity across conditions, formulations, and study designs limits interpretation. Across compounds, mechanistic plausibility generally exceeds evidence of clinical efficacy and direct target engagement in humans. Future studies should prioritize standardized formulations, clinically relevant outcomes, adequate follow-up, safety assessment, and mechanistic biomarkers within phenotype-informed pain management.

title: Reward-Based Eating Drive Is Associated with Distinct Resting-State Connectivity Patterns: A RED-13 and fMRI Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Eating for pleasure rather than hunger is widespread in the modern food environment. The Reward-Based Eating Drive Scale (RED-13) captures three dimensions of reward-related eating: lack of satiety, loss of control over eating, and preoccupation with food. This cross-sectional study aimed to evaluate the relationship between resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) metrics and the RED-13 subscales. Methods: RED-13 scores, subjective food appetite, and resting-state brain function were measured in 99 participants between March 2022 and May 2023. Brain function was assessed using degree centrality (DC), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and voxel-mirrored homotopic connectivity (VMHC). Results: Loss of control over eating and preoccupation with food positively correlated with appetite for high fat, high sweet, and low sweet foods. Loss of control over eating positively correlated with DC in the left cerebellar lobule IX (r = 0.416), ReHo in the left brainstem (r = 0.399), and VMHC in the right and left brainstem (r = 0.432) and negatively with ReHo in the right calcarine sulcus (r = -0.434). The lack of satiety subscale positively correlated with ReHo in the left superior frontal gyrus (r = 0.389). The preoccupation with food subscale positively correlated with DC and ReHo in the right middle frontal gyrus. Conclusions: Reward-based eating measured by RED-13 is associated with distinct patterns in the resting-state fMRI metrics within reward processing and cognitive control. These neural correlates, supported by the association of RED-13 with appetite, are consistent with the hypothesis that RED-13 captures a trait-like disposition toward reward-driven eating that might be reflected in the resting-state brain activity.

title: A Scoping Review of Creatine Supplementation in Alzheimer's Disease: Evidence from Preclinical and Clinical Studies.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Although creatine supplementation has a theoretical rationale for neuroprotection, public interest has outpaced available scientific evidence. Alzheimer's disease (AD), a major and growing global health concern, is among the neurodegenerative diseases proposed to benefit from creatine supplementation. This scoping review systematically maps the existing literature on creatine supplementation for AD to identify gaps that limit translational progress. Methods: Following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a search in five electronic databases was conducted for preclinical and clinical studies evaluating creatine interventions in AD. The methodological quality of the studies was appraised using the SYRCLE and NIH tools, respectively. Results: Nine unique studies were included. The preclinical models investigated neuron apoptosis, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial function, cognitive outcomes, and pathophysiological clearance. Conversely, clinical studies were limited to a pilot trial that suggested preliminary tolerability but could not establish causality. This review identifies six limitations within the current evidence: (1) a reliance on acute or non-transgenic animal models that lack construct validity; (2) a need to address sexual dimorphism; (3) a lack of studies exploring administration routes to bypass the blood-brain barrier; (4) a complete lack of independent randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with all clinical evidence originating from a single research group; (5) an absence of research assessing creatine as a preventive strategy; and (6) a shortage of assessment regarding physical syndromes, such as frailty. Conclusions: The scientific evidence for creatine in AD remains preliminary. Future research should prioritize progressive transgenic models, evaluate noninvasive administration routes, investigate effects on frailty, assess long-term preventive efficacy, account for sex as a variable, and transition to rigorous RCTs.

title: Potential Benefits and Limitations of Hericium erinaceus Supplementation.
abstract: Hericium erinaceus (Lion's Mane) is an edible and medicinal mushroom that has attracted increasing scientific interest as a dietary supplement because of its potential effects on cognitive function, neuroprotection, mental well-being and healthy ageing. Its biological activities have been primarily attributed to bioactive compounds such as polysaccharides, hericenones and erinacines, which may influence neurotrophic signalling, neuroplasticity, oxidative stress, inflammation and neuronal survival. This review examines the potential benefits and limitations of H. erinaceus supplementation, with emphasis on its bioactive compounds, mechanisms of action, cognitive and neuroprotective effects, mental-health-related outcomes, safety and product quality. Experimental studies provide evidence for neurotrophic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective activities, while clinical studies suggest possible benefits for cognitive outcomes, particularly information-processing speed, subjective stress and well-being. However, findings are inconsistent across study populations and outcomes, and evidence regarding neurodegenerative diseases is still largely derived from preclinical studies. Interpretation is further complicated by small sample sizes, short intervention periods, variability in supplement formulations, differences between fruiting-body-derived and mycelium-derived preparations and insufficient standardisation of bioactive compounds. Although H. erinaceus supplementation is generally well tolerated, its safety during prolonged use and optimal dosage remains unclear. Overall, H. erinaceus shows potential as a dietary supplement for supporting cognitive and neurological health, but further well-designed clinical trials involving larger populations, longer intervention periods and standardised, well-characterised preparations are needed to confirm its clinical effectiveness and establish reliable recommendations for safe supplementation.

title: Gut Microbial Levodopa Metabolism and Constipation in Prodromal and Established Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Background: Constipation can precede the motor diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD), but its mechanisms are multifactorial. Gut bacteria can metabolize administered levodopa (LD), and enteric dopamine receptors participate in the regulation of motility. These observations motivate, but do not establish, a connection between microbial LD metabolism and constipation. Evidence: Bacterial tyrosine decarboxylase (TDC) converts LD to dopamine in biochemical and animal systems. Human studies associate fecal TDC abundance with some treatment and pharmacokinetic variables, but gene abundance does not measure enzyme activity. A longitudinal PD cohort found an inverse association between constipation severity and TDC abundance in one model, highlighting the need to consider medication effects and reverse causation. Microbiome alterations in risk-enriched populations do not demonstrate increased TDC activity before PD diagnosis. Hypothesis: In a subset of untreated individuals at increased risk of PD, sufficient luminal endogenous L-DOPA might permit microbial dopamine production that influences intestinal transit, provided that the resulting dopamine reaches relevant receptors at effective concentrations. Endogenous substrate availability, anatomical access, and the net balance of dopamine production and clearance are unresolved. After LD treatment begins, a larger exogenous substrate supply creates a distinct setting for drug-microbe interactions. Conclusions: The proposed continuum is conditional and requires biochemical and functional validation before human biomarker development. We propose substrate tracing, comparisons of TDC-positive and TDC-deficient bacteria, receptor-specific testing, and longitudinal gastrointestinal phenotyping. Current evidence does not justify TDC-directed dietary prevention of PD or clinical prediction from fecal TDC abundance alone.

title: Intranasal Chitosan Nano-Formulations: A Novel Frontier in Brain Cancer Therapy.
abstract: Direct nose-to-brain drug delivery is emerging as a promising approach in neuro-oncology because it offers a non-invasive, needle-free route for delivering therapeutics to the brain while partially bypassing the blood-brain barrier (BBB). This approach takes advantage of the natural connections between the nasal cavity and the central nervous system, allowing drugs administered through the nose to reach brain tissues through the olfactory and trigeminal pathways. Despite its potential, successful clinical translation remains challenging because the nasal cavity presents several physiological barriers. Mucus can trap drug molecules, mucociliary clearance can rapidly remove them, and nasal enzymes can degrade them before they reach their target. Advanced nanocarrier systems are therefore being developed to overcome these barriers and improve drug transport through intracellular, paracellular, and transcellular pathways. In this context, specific structural modifications can enhance drug retention, mucus penetration, cellular uptake, and targeting efficiency. Important strategies include the use of mucoadhesive materials such as chitosan to increase residence time in the nasal cavity; hydrophilic coatings such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) to improve movement through mucus; targeting ligands to promote selective cellular uptake; and stimuli-responsive systems that respond to local conditions such as pH, redox state, or glutathione (GSH) levels. These advances are particularly relevant to the treatment of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), one of the most aggressive and difficult-to-treat brain tumors. GBM is characterized by extensive infiltration into surrounding healthy brain tissue, making it difficult to achieve effective drug concentrations throughout both the main tumor mass and its invasive margins. Intranasally delivered chitosan-based nano-formulations may help address this problem through a series of transport steps. After administration, the nanoparticles can interact with and remain within the nasal mucosa, move across the olfactory epithelium, and pass through the cribriform plate toward the olfactory bulb. From there, they may distribute into deeper regions of the brain and potentially increase drug accumulation within both the GBM core and infiltrative tumor regions. This review presents a structured overview of engineered chitosan nano-formulations for targeted drug delivery in neuro-oncology. It focuses on their physicochemical properties, mechanisms of nose-to-brain transport, drug-loading strategies, tumor-targeting approaches, therapeutic applications, and the major challenges that must be addressed before clinical translation. Overall, these systems offer a promising strategy for improving the precision and effectiveness of drug delivery to brain tumors and may contribute to the development of more targeted treatments for GBM and other neurological malignancies.

title: Leakage-Controlled Deep Learning for Multi-Analyte Classification and Quantification in Fast-Scan Cyclic Voltammetry.
abstract: Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) is a widely used electrochemical technique for real-time monitoring of neurotransmitters; however, quantitative interpretation remains dependent on calibration curves generated in simplified in vitro environments that may not accurately reflect the complexity of biological matrices. To address the need for automated FSCV interpretation, we developed a two-stage artificial intelligence (AI) framework integrating analyte classification and concentration prediction. FSCV data were collected for serotonin (5-HT), dopamine (DA), ascorbic acid (AA), and copper (Cu2+) using analyte-specific waveforms, generating a dataset of 30,811 cyclic voltammograms from 192 independent experimental runs. Classification models were evaluated using strict run-level partitioning, while regression performance was additionally assessed using run-level and leave-one-electrode-out (LOEO) validation. Four classification architectures were evaluated: a lightweight image-based convolutional neural network (CNN), a feature-engineered multilayer perceptron (MLP), a transfer-learning ResNet18 model, and a one-dimensional CNN (1D-CNN) trained directly on raw voltammograms. The 1D-CNN achieved the highest classification accuracy (99.8%), outperforming transfer learning (98.68%), the lightweight CNN (97.38%), and the feature-based MLP (76.3 ± 0.6%) while maintaining substantially lower model complexity than ResNet18. Input-channel ablation indicated that waveform-specific acquisition protocols contributed to classification performance. For quantitative analysis, analyte-specific artificial neural networks (ANNs) were trained to predict concentrations from voltammetric morphology, achieving coefficients of determination (R2) of 0.9958, 0.9970, 0.9849, and 0.9561 for 5-HT, DA, Cu2+, and AA, respectively, under the original random sample-level partitioning. However, mean R2 values decreased to 0.74-0.88 under run-level validation and 0.61-0.86 under LOEO validation, with conventional peak-current calibration outperforming the ANNs under LOEO conditions. Integration of classification and regression models into an automated inference pipeline enabled sequential analyte identification and concentration estimation from FSCV data. In an additional end-to-end evaluation using the 1D-CNN classifier and analyte-specific ANN regressors, incorrect analyte routing, although infrequent (approximately 0.8%), produced substantial concentration-prediction errors. These results demonstrate the potential of morphology-aware deep learning for automated FSCV interpretation while highlighting the need for improved quantitative reliability and further validation using independent electrodes, mixed-analyte samples, and complex biological matrices.

title: Triboelectric Sensory Intelligence: From Mechanical Information Encoding to In-Sensor Memory, Neuromorphic Computing, and Closed-Loop Interaction.
abstract: Triboelectric interfaces are progressing beyond self-powered sensing toward integrated sensory systems capable of encoding, retaining, transforming, and responding to mechanical information. Yet, the rapid convergence of triboelectric transduction with memory, neuromorphic devices, and intelligent interfaces has also blurred the distinctions between signal generation, state modulation, physical computation, and task-level intelligence. This Review establishes an information-centric framework for triboelectric sensory intelligence, in which mechanical interaction is traced through electrical encoding, signal-device coupling, internal state evolution, sensory processing, perception, and ultimately closed-loop action. Sensory representations based on amplitude, polarity, temporal structure, spatial patterns, material-dependent responses, and multimodal signals are considered in terms of encoding fidelity, separability, and robustness. Stateful mechanisms based on resistive switching, charge storage, ferroelectric polarization, and ionic or electrochemical dynamics are then related to sensory memory, temporal filtering, synaptic plasticity, event-based transformation, and other physical computational primitives. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing structural integration from processing location, device dynamics from implemented computation, and hardware processing from downstream software inference. The Review further links these principles to tactile and material perception, gesture and motion interfaces, multisensory integration, and sensory-motor feedback, while introducing system-level considerations of reproducibility, energy, latency, scalability, and generalization. Looking forward, reliable source-receiver co-design, adaptive processing, scalable heterogeneous integration, and closed-loop operation will be central to translating triboelectric interfaces from isolated device demonstrations into persistent and autonomous sensory systems.

title: An ESP32-S3 Multimodal Wearable Sensor Platform with Embedded XGBoost for Focal-to-Bilateral Tonic-Clonic Seizure Detection and IoT Alerting.
abstract: Wearable seizure-detection systems can provide objective event monitoring and rapid caregiver alerting without continuous bedside observation. This study presents a resource-constrained multimodal wearable sensor platform for focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (FBTCS) detection using edge artificial intelligence and Internet of Things (IoT) communication. The prototype integrates an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, an analog electromyography (EMG) channel, an MPU6050 inertial sensor, MAX30102 photoplethysmography, GPS, a TFT display, local vibration/buzzer outputs, and Blynk cloud telemetry. The seizure-decision path uses synchronized EMG and acceleration acquired at 100 Hz in non-overlapping 10 s windows. EMG and acceleration are resampled for compatibility with the reference feature pipeline, 13 statistical features are extracted from each modality (26 total), and an 85-tree XGBoost model is executed locally. A probability threshold of 0.85 is combined with temporal smoothing, consecutive-window confirmation, and a 60 s refractory interval. Software verification showed maximum absolute probability differences of approximately 1.19 × 10-7 for random feature-vector tests and 1.49 × 10-8 for end-to-end recorded windows relative to the Python reference. Within the reported validation record covering 2643.69 h and 18 record-labeled FBTCS events, 12 events were detected (12/18; 67% sensitivity). Precision was approximately 26%, F1-score approximately 38%, the reported false-alarm rate was 0.31 per 24 h, and median detection latency was 61.5 s. Approximately 34 false alarms are estimated from the reported false-alarm rate and evaluation duration; this is an estimated count rather than a percentage or directly observed count. Hardware, local alarm, display, GPS, and cloud communication functions passed functional integration tests. The small event count, uncertain label provenance, low precision, and long latency mean that these data support an engineering proof-of-concept only and do not establish clinical applicability.

title: Toward Robust and Reliable Muscle Synergy Analysis: A Methodological Survey of Synergy Extraction.
abstract: Muscle synergy analysis has been widely applied in neuroscience, biomechanics, rehabilitation, and robotics. However, the reliability of muscle synergy extraction remains a critical issue, as results are highly sensitive to variations in experimental design, surface electromyography preprocessing, factorization algorithms, and the determination of the number of synergies. This narrative methodological review examines the key factors that influence the robustness and reliability of muscle synergies within the framework of limb neuromechanical controllers across anatomical regions and task contexts. By analyzing the current state of research in this field, we first summarize the conceptual and methodological foundations of muscle synergy analysis and then critically examine the factors that influence its robustness and reliability. This review provides practical recommendations to enhance methodological rigor, including greater methodological harmonization and transparent reporting of experimental protocols, the use of musculoskeletal simulation to evaluate muscle selection strategies, and the refinement of synergy extraction techniques. These insights aim to improve the reliability and robustness of muscle synergy analysis and promote its application in robotics, human-machine interfacing, and computational motor control.

title: Harnessing Nanozyme Catalytic Activities for Multi-Target Intervention in Neurodegenerative Pathology.
abstract: The therapeutic landscape for neurodegenerative diseases (NDs), including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, remains challenging due to their complex, multifactorial pathogenesis and the limited efficacy of conventional therapies that primarily offer symptomatic relief. The emergence of nanozymes, nanomaterials with intrinsic enzyme-mimicking activities, presents a promising opportunity for multi-targeted intervention. This review comprehensively explores the rational design and therapeutic mechanisms of nanozymes in combating core pathological features of NDs, such as oxidative stress, protein aggregation, and neuroinflammation. We critically assess their remarkable ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and execute synergistic functions, including reactive oxygen species scavenging, misfolded protein degradation, and modulation of microglial activation. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the application and efficacy of nanozymes across major NDs, alongside a discussion on pharmacokinetics, biosafety, and prevailing challenges. By delineating the structure-enzyme-mimicking activity relationships and cellular-level mechanisms, this review aims to establish a foundational framework for the future development of nanozyme-based neuroprotective strategies, supporting ongoing efforts toward disease-modifying interventions for NDs.

title: Secondary Metabolites from Mariana Trench-Derived Penicillium sp. SCSIO41052 and Their Antimicrobial Activity.
abstract: Compared to terrestrial environments, marine ecosystems are characterized by dynamic environmental conditions such as temperature, salinity, pressure. As major producers of marine natural products, marine-derived fungi thrive in these extreme habitats, leading to produce secondary metabolites with unprecedented chemical structures and unique bioactivities. In this study, two new linear N-acetylpeptides (1 and 2) and one new long-chain carboxylic acid (3) along with fifteen known compounds were isolated from Penicillium sp. SCSIO41052 separated from Mariana Trench sediment. Their structures were elucidated through spectroscopic analysis. Marfey's analysis of the hydrolysate of 1 was performed to determine the absolute configurations of its amino acid residues. By comparing the ECD curves of 1 and 2, it can be concluded that they have identical absolute configurations. The activity screening indicated that eight compounds (3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 13 and 18) exhibited antimicrobial activity. Notably, compound 13 exhibited varying levels of antimicrobial activity against six pathogenic strains with Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) values ranging from 0.5 to 64 μg/mL, highlighting its potential antimicrobial properties. Moreover, compound 2 displayed moderate cytotoxic activity against the PC3 cell line. Compound 5 showed weak acetylcholinesterase (AchE) inhibition. These findings not only enriched the chemical structural diversity of secondary metabolites from marine fungi but also explored potential bioactive molecules, thereby laying a foundation for further research on marine medicinal resources.

title: Integrated Biochemical and Computational Evaluation of Bis-Imidazolium Derivatives 3e-3g in Cholinesterase and HIV-1 Reverse Transcriptase Assays.
abstract: Bis-imidazolium derivatives (3e, 3f, 3g) were evaluated for their inhibitory activity against acetylcholinesterase (AChE), butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), and human immunodeficiency virus type 1 reverse transcriptase (HIV-1 RT) using colorimetric assays and molecular docking. For the HIV-1 RT-3e complex, a 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area (MM/GBSA) analysis were performed. Compound 3e emerged as the most active derivative, showing the lowest half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values: 13.36 µg/mL for AChE, 4.95 µg/mL for BChE, and 50.44 µg/mL for HIV-1 RT. Nevirapine produced 95.33% RT inhibition at 20 µM. Redocking validated the binding poses with root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) values below 2.0 Å, though docking scores lacked consistent correlation with experimental activity rankings. In the MD trajectory, 3e remained stable within the RT binding pocket, yielding an MM/GBSA energy of -51.04 ± 8.39 kcal/mol. Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) predictions indicated low gastrointestinal absorption, no blood-brain barrier permeation, and a high-confidence human ether-à-go-go-related gene (hERG) potassium channel blockade alert. These findings highlight 3e for further optimization.

title: Synthesis, Hydration, Antibacterial, Antifungal, and Antiviral Properties of New Surface-Active Nicotine-Based Ionic Liquids.
abstract: Nicotine is a pyridine alkaloid naturally produced by plants of the Solanaceae family. In this study, four nicotine-based ionic liquids (ILs) with different alkyl side-chain lengths were synthesized by alkylation with alkyl bromides: N-octylnicotinium bromide, N-decylnicotinium bromide, N-dodecylnicotinium bromide, and N-tetradecylnicotinium bromide; of these, only the octyl derivative was previously reported. Their structures were confirmed by NMR spectroscopy. All ILs were water-soluble within the investigated concentration range and exhibited surfactant properties. Critical micelle concentrations (CMC) were determined by conductometry, while density, sound velocity, and viscosity measurements were used to investigate hydration behavior. CMC values decreased with increasing alkyl chain length, indicating enhanced aggregation, while all ILs exhibited structure-making effects in water. Antimicrobial activity was evaluated against three Gram-positive and three Gram-negative bacterial species, four mold species, two yeast species, and five bacteriophage species. The ILs showed substantially greater antimicrobial activity than nicotine. Antibacterial activity increased with alkyl chain length, and longer-chain ILs outperformed a commercial disinfectant, benzalkonium chloride, in selected antibacterial and antiviral assays. Antifungal activity was comparable to or slightly lower than that of benzalkonium chloride, depending on the species. N-tetradecylnicotinium bromide exhibited the strongest antiviral activity. These results demonstrate a clear relationship between IL structure, aggregation behavior, hydration properties, and antimicrobial activity.

title: PARAFAC-Assisted Excitation-Emission Matrix Fluorescence for Minimal-Preparation Co-Determination of Norfloxacin and Metoclopramide in Human Urine: Overcoming Severe Concentration Imbalance Without Chromatography.
abstract: Direct simultaneous determination of norfloxacin (NOR) and metoclopramide (MET) in human urine is severely complicated by intense biological autofluorescence, spectral overlap, and an extreme concentration disparity arising from clinical co-administration (400 mg NOR vs. 10 mg MET; dose ratio 40:1). Multiway chemometrics offers a chromatography-free approach to resolving fluorophores, but biological background and extreme concentration disparities can complicate global PARAFAC modeling. Herein, we demonstrate that this limitation can be completely overcome using a dual-submatrix excitation-emission matrix (EEM) PARAFAC strategy in human urine after a simple 10-fold dilution with pH 3.0 aqueous buffer, omitting extraction, derivatization, and organic solvents. By partitioning the measured EEM array into two dedicated sub-arrays (XNOR: λex 260-310 nm, λem 440-500 nm; XMET: λex 260-310 nm, λem 380-410 nm), rank deficiency is circumvented, rotational ambiguity is eliminated, and trilinearity is fully preserved. External calibration in spiked urine yielded linear dynamic ranges of 1000-6000 ng mL-1 for NOR (R2 = 0.9981) and 15-80 ng mL-1 for MET (R2 = 0.9995). Validation across independent test mixtures showed excellent mean recoveries of 100.79 ± 4.57% for NOR and 101.86 ± 4.06% for MET, with root mean square errors of prediction (RMSEP) of 144.65 and 2.38 ng mL-1, respectively. Net analyte signal figures of merit demonstrated high sensitivity and limits of detection of 119.87 ng mL-1 (NOR) and 3.16 ng mL-1 (MET). The validated method was successfully applied to urinary excretion monitoring in five healthy volunteers following oral co-administration of commercial tablets (Noracin® 400 mg and Primperan® 10 mg), recovering 24.89 ± 4.63% (NOR) and 13.59 ± 9.27% (MET) of the administered dose over 72 h. Multi-metric greenness and practicality assessments (AGREE: 0.68, ComplexMoGAPI: 69, CaFRI: 63.1, BAGI: 75.0) confirmed substantial sustainability advantages over conventional chromatographic workflows. This study revitalizes PARAFAC as an ultra-green, chromatography-free tool for modern pharmaceutical bioanalysis.

title: Design and Synthesis of New Derivatives of Alkaloid Lupinine: Structural Characterization, Acetylcholinesterase Inhibition Evaluation, and Molecular Modeling Study.
abstract: Plant alkaloids have been of great interest in drug development research. Alkaloid lupinine is of great interest because of its availability and biological activity. While several lupinine derivatives have been identified with specific biological activities, the ongoing challenge lies in the design and synthesis of novel derivatives with high specificity for additional pharmacological targets. This paper describes the synthesis of lupinine derivatives as acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitors. Two approaches were proposed and implemented for the synthesis of new compounds (yields 71-90%): the CuAAC reaction of lupinyl azide with a series of prop-2-ynyl- and ethynyl-substituted alkaloid derivatives, and a copper-catalyzed one-pot three-component reaction (A3-coupling) involving 1-((prop-2-ynyloxy)methyl)octahydro-1H-quinolizine, formaldehyde, and secondary amines. The biological activity of the new compounds was evaluated using the Ellman method; the results showed that most of the synthesized substances demonstrated good or moderate inhibitory activity against acetylcholinesterase in vitro. Hybrid compounds containing lupinine and xanthine fragments (theophylline, caffeine) 11, 12, or colchicine 15, as well as the bis-lupinyl derivative 16, exhibited the highest inhibitory activity against AChE with IC50 values of 0.47, 0.035, 1.3, and 1.4 μM, respectively. The binding conformation and simultaneous interaction modes were further clarified by molecular docking studies.

title: Molecular Diagnostic Biomarkers in Autism Spectrum Disorder: From Multi-Omics Signatures to Precision Therapeutic Targets.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a systemic multi-organ condition characterized by profound biological heterogeneity. Clinical management currently faces a bottleneck due to reliance on subjective behavioral phenotyping rather than objective molecular markers. This review synthesizes breakthroughs in ASD diagnostics, moving from a reductionist "one-size-fits-all" approach toward an integrative systems biology framework. We evaluate how genetic variants and epigenetic modifications converge on shared pathways, such as synaptic homeostasis and chromatin remodeling. Furthermore, we highlight the diagnostic potential of proteomic and metabolomic signatures, which capture functional states more proximally to the clinical phenotype, including sex-specific metabotypes. The roles of neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and the gut-microbiota-brain axis are delineated as key contributing factors of pathophysiology. Finally, we propose a roadmap for integrating multi-omics data via machine learning to facilitate early screening and precision therapeutic stratification. By bridging molecular footprints with clinical phenotyping, this synthesis provides a foundation for personalized medicine in neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Flavonoids from Pyrus communis L. 'Kashi': Isolation, Structural Identification, NO Inhibitory Activity, and Molecular Docking.
abstract: Pyrus communis L. 'Kashi', a Xinjiang pear cultivar, is traditionally consumed after baking to alleviate inflammation-related ailments, although its active constituents remain unclear. Flavonoids were isolated chromatographically and identified by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and high-resolution electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (HR-ESI-MS). Cytotoxicity and nitric oxide (NO) inhibition were evaluated in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages using 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) and Griess assays, respectively. Docking was performed with inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). Eleven flavonoids were isolated and identified; four were isolated and NMR-characterized from Pyrus for the first time. Cell viability remained above 60% at 100 μM. Apigenin, kaempferol, and isorhamnetin-3-O-galactoside showed the strongest NO-inhibitory effects, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 22.75 ± 3.23, 37.54 ± 4.40, and 58.19 ± 10.41 μM, respectively. Preliminary structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis suggested that reduced hydroxylation in compounds 1-3 and shorter sugar chains among the glycosides examined tended to be associated with lower normalized NO levels; Isorhamnetin-3-O-galactoside was more active than the corresponding glucoside. Docking revealed differences in predicted ligand orientation and residue interactions, providing complementary qualitative structural information. These findings expand the flavonoid profile of P. communis L. 'Kashi' and highlight preliminary NO-inhibitory SAR trends.

title: Curcumin, Resveratrol and Berberine as Emerging Therapeutic Agents in Treatment of Gliomas: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: Brain tumors represent a major clinical challenge due to their complex biology, inherent resistance to conventional therapies and the limited delivery of anticancer agents across the blood-brain barrier. Natural phytochemicals such as curcumin, resveratrol and berberine have gained increasing attention for their multi-targeted anticancer properties, including induction of apoptosis, inhibition of proliferation, suppression of mitochondrial and BCL-2-family signaling and modulation of the tumor microenvironment. This comprehensive review critically examines current evidence on the use of curcumin, resveratrol and berberine in the context of brain tumor treatment, with an emphasis on gliomas' mechanisms of action, pharmacokinetic limitations, and potential for integration into novel delivery platforms. We discuss how these compounds interact with key pathways in brain tumors-including BCL-2 inhibition, PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and epigenetic regulation-and the emerging strategies to overcome glioma-specific obstacles such as blood-brain barrier permeability and microenvironmental hypoxia. Furthermore, the review explores innovative formulations and carrier systems that enhance brain uptake and bioavailability of these agents, bridging the gap between preclinical promise and clinical translation. By identifying current gaps and proposing future research directions, this article aims to provide a roadmap for harnessing curcumin, resveratrol and berberine as adjuvant or combinatorial treatments in brain tumor therapy, focusing particularly on glioma treatment. The adoption of such phytochemicals may open new avenues for improved outcomes in patients with highly refractory brain malignancies.

title: Curcumin Prevents Degeneration of Medial Septal Cholinergic Neurons Produced by Parkinsonism-Inducing Neurotoxin 1-Methyl-4-Phenylpyridinium.
abstract: The neurotoxin 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine is converted into the active metabolite 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+), which damages dopamine (DA)-containing neurons of Substantia Nigra, and norepinephrine (NE)-containing neurons of Locus Coeruleus, thus mimicking the pathology of Parkinson's disease (PD). In PD, cognitive impairment often occurs, which may be due to a loss of acetylcholine (ACh)-containing neurons within the basal forebrain. In turn, this may result from either direct damage to ACh neurons or indirect damage through loss of their DA and/or NE innervation. In the present study, we used neurons from the medial septal nucleus (MSN), which grow in the absence of DA or NE innervation, to assess the direct effects of MPP+ on MSN-derived ACh neurons. Administration of MPP+ directly damages MSN-derived neurons, as evidenced by neuronal loss and dramatic mitochondrial alterations. The phytochemical curcumin administered before MPP+ prevents ACh neuronal damage and mitochondrial derangement. Curcumin administration following MPP+ still promotes neuronal survival while reshaping both damaged mitochondria and cellular processes of ACh neurons. These latter effects are consistent with the expression of key proteins such as PINK1, Parkin, and LC3-II and activation of autophagy flux.

title: Quercetin Alleviates Chronic Post-Ischemia Pain in Rats and Inhibits NaV1.7 Sodium Channels.
abstract: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome type I (CRPS-I) poses a formidable challenge in pain management due to its debilitating symptoms and a lack of effective, targeted therapies. The chronic post-ischemia pain (CPIP) rodent model, which recapitulates the ischemia-reperfusion injury implicated in CRPS-I, provides a robust platform for exploring novel interventions. While quercetin (Que), a natural flavonoid, is recognized for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, its specific therapeutic efficacy and molecular targets in CRPS-I remain largely unknown. In this study, we evaluated the therapeutic potential of Que in addressing CRPS-related neuropathic pain using the CPIP model. Behavioral assessments revealed that Que significantly attenuates mechanical allodynia and cold hypersensitivity in CPIP rats. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we investigated Que's impact on peripheral nociceptive signaling. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrated that Que markedly suppresses tetrodotoxin-sensitive (TTX-S) sodium currents in isolated dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. To pinpoint the exact molecular target, we further evaluated Que in a heterologous expression system, confirming that it selectively inhibits Nav1.7 channel currents in transfected HEK293 cells. In addition to its known anti-inflammatory profile, our in vitro findings reveal that Que selectively modulates the Nav1.7 channel, providing new insights into its pleiotropic pharmacological characteristics. By bridging macroscopic analgesic phenotypes with a microscopic channel-blocking mechanism, this study establishes Que as a promising, safe, non-opioid candidate for CRPS-I translational therapy.

title: Potential Mechanisms of Chlorogenic Acid in Cognitive Impairment: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a clinical syndrome primarily affecting cognitive functions such as learning, memory, perception, and problem-solving. Its causes are heterogeneous, including neurological, psychiatric, metabolic, vascular, toxicological, and age-related factors. Currently, no specific and effective pharmacological therapies are available for CI in clinical practice. As one of the most abundant dietary polyphenols, chlorogenic acid (CGA) displays diverse biological effects and has recently garnered growing interest within cognitive neuroscience. This review summarizes the mechanisms by which CGA ameliorates cognitive impairment, encompassing neuroprotection, modulation of the gut-brain axis, inhibition of neuroinflammation, inhibition of oxidative stress, promotion of autophagy, inhibition of apoptosis, and suppression of amyloid-β (Aβ) formation. The signaling pathways implicated include activation of the PKC, Nrf2/PPAR and Nrf2/ARE pathways, as well as inhibition of the TLR4/NF-κB, mTOR/TFEB, p38 MAPK, and JNK/c-Jun pathways. This article provides an overview of current advancements in CGA, addressing its chemical attributes, dietary origins, drug metabolism, and the mechanistic basis for its efficacy in neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Chemical Composition and Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitory Activity of the Volatile Fraction from the Ecuadorian Moss Sphagnum magellanicum Brid.
abstract: The volatile fraction (VF) of the aerial parts of Sphagnum magellanicum Brid. (Sphagnaceae), collected in southern Ecuador (2740 m a.s.l), was obtained for the first time by steam distillation using a Dean-Stark adapted apparatus and characterized by gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and flame ionization detection (GC-FID). A total of 89 compounds representing 95.28 ± 1.95% of the total VF were identified. The predominant chemical classes were n-alkanes (39.94%), alcohols (17.56%), sesquiterpene hydrocarbons (13.10%), and oxygenated sesquiterpenes (6.48%). Phytol was the major single compound (16.09 ± 0.07%), followed by n-tricosane (9.25 ± 0.82%), n-heneicosane (9.17 ± 0.54%), hexacosane (7.30 ± 0.99%), nonacosane (5.42 ± 0.14%), (Z)-caryophyllene (4.08 ± 0.32%), hexadecanoic acid (3.64 ± 0.25%), and dotriacontane (2.93 ± 0.21%). The VF was evaluated in vitro for acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitory activity using the Ellman colorimetric assay, yielding a moderate inhibitory effect with an IC50 value of 77.0 ± 1.03 µg/mL. These results provide the first phytochemical and pharmacological characterization of S. magellanicum from Ecuador, establishing it as a potential source of bioactive volatile constituents with potential relevance for further pharmacological investigation.

title: Sim-SEA: Integrating Significant Event Audit and In Situ Simulation to Support Patient Safety Learning and Organizational Change-A Prospective Single-Center Pilot Study in Pediatric Emergency Care.
abstract: Patient safety depends on healthcare systems' ability to learn from clinical experience and translate insights into system-level improvement. Significant Event Audit (SEA) is well established but may only partly capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of clinical performance. Although in situ simulation is increasingly used to explore team performance and system vulnerabilities, its routine integration into formal risk-management pathways remains limited. We developed Sim-SEA, a structured approach embedding in situ simulation within the SEA learning cycle. Sim-SEA adapted the seven-phase SEA framework to incorporate in situ simulation as a core component. We conducted a 12-month single-center, uncontrolled pre-post pilot study in a tertiary pediatric emergency department, comprising 10 Sim-SEA cycles. Self-perceived competence in technical and non-technical domains was assessed at baseline and immediately after simulation using a 6-item ad hoc questionnaire. A follow-up assessment was conducted among participants who subsequently encountered a real emergency. Participants' perceptions, system vulnerabilities, and improvement actions were also examined. Fifty-nine physicians, residents, and nurses participated. Self-perceived competence improved significantly from baseline to post-simulation across ABCDE assessment, teamwork, situational awareness, communication, speak-up behavior, and decision-making (all p < 0.01). At follow-up, available for 35/59 participants (59.3%) who subsequently encountered a real emergency, self-perceived scores remained significantly higher than baseline. Implemented changes included workspace reorganization, a cognitive medication aid, and a standard operating procedure for role allocation. Participants reported greater engagement, reflective learning, psychological safety, and awareness of risks and system vulnerabilities. In this single-center, uncontrolled pilot study, Sim-SEA was feasible as a structured method for embedding in situ simulation within clinical risk management and supported potential benefits for self-perceived learning and the identification and development of organizational and environmental improvement actions. Further studies should assess effects on objective competence and patient-safety outcomes.

title: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency in Primary Care: A Scoping Review of Recognition, Diagnostic Delay and Interdisciplinary Care Pathways.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) affects approximately 3.5% of women with lifelong bone, cardiovascular, psychological and reproductive consequences. International guidance assigns primary care important roles in recognition, diagnosis and follow-up. This review mapped evidence across the POI care continuum. Methods: Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched from inception to 4 October 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records and assessed full texts. Data were charted by one reviewer, verified by a second and synthesised across five domains.
